title: Fundamentals of Organizing: Why Do Firms Exist?
sources: M01 Handout + Post-Lecture Slides BA-A (39 p.)
Bieger et al. (2021), An Introduction to Management Studies, Ch. 1.2–1.3 (SGMM)

bigPicture: Business administration starts from one goal: **creating value**, by transforming resources into products, services and solutions that customers value more than they cost.
Value creation happens inside a **system of stakeholders and environmental spheres** (St. Gallen Management Model) and along **integrated value chains**.
Firms exist because needs exceed resources and **division of labour and specialization** raise productivity (Smith, Ford, Taylor).
But division of labour creates **costs of organizing**: **coordination problems** (bullwhip effect) and **motivation problems**.

**Transaction cost economics** (Coase, Williamson) explains **make-or-buy**: a transaction is done in the firm (hierarchy) or on the market depending on where costs are lower; **asset specificity, uncertainty and frequency** raise hold-up risk (Tesla's vertical integration).

concepts.name: Course structure and exam
concepts.simple: The course has lectures (theory), exercise classes (cases), self-study (a running case) and touchpoints (submitted team work). One big exam at the end decides everything.
exam: Four pillars: **lectures** (terminology, foundational theories), **exercise groups** (knowledge application, link to practice), **self-study** (running case, deepening), **touchpoints/teamwork** (transfer, complex problem-solving).

Five content areas: **organizing** (why do firms exist? how do they build value systems?), **strategy** (capture value), **innovation** (create value), **marketing** (deliver value), **supply chain** (orchestrate value), plus integration.
Exercise cases: N26 (PBL 1), L'Oréal (PBL 2), Weisse Arena (PBL 3–5), Appenzeller (PBL 6); running case **ON** (touchpoints 1–5, due Tuesdays 23:59 on Canvas).

**Exam:** two-part, digital, on-campus written exam on **26 January**: **180 minutes, 180 points, 100 % of the grade**. Lecture part: **closed-ended questions** on core learning objectives. Tutorial part: **case-based** (unfamiliar company), **5 tasks** along the content blocks.
concepts.example: The final lecture (W12) includes a mock exam (NORDIC HOME).

concepts.name: Value creation: the goal of business administration
concepts.simple: A bakery turns flour, work and an oven into bread people love. If people value the bread more than everything it cost to make, the bakery has created value.
exam: “Prosperity is not a matter of chance. It does not simply arise from the availability of resources. It is the result of a specific process: **value creation**.”
- **Value creation process:** **resources** (labour, capital, knowledge, materials) → **transformation process** → **output** (products, services, solutions) → **perceived value**.
- **Value = the benefit that customers attribute to a product, minus the costs of all the steps required to produce it.**
- The value creation process defines the **sub-disciplines**: research & development, strategy, marketing, operations, accounting & control, organizational behaviour.
concepts.example: Mock exam Q1: ‘value’ is NOT the market price; it is customer benefit minus the costs of all production steps.

concepts.name: Integrated value chains and business research
concepts.simple: A car is made by a long chain of firms: steel maker, tyre maker, parts maker, the car brand, the transport company and the dealer.
concepts.exam: Automotive example of an **integrated value chain**: ArcelorMittal (steel for the car body) → Continental (tyres) → Bosch (modules) → **Mercedes-Benz (OEM)** → DB Schenker (logistics) → Emil Frey (auto dealer). Trade has existed for thousands of years (e.g. the **Fugger** family), but the **systematic, scientific analysis** of how business works began **just over a century ago**. Key questions: how can companies operate more productively? Why are some more successful than others?
concepts.example: OEM = original equipment manufacturer: the firm that assembles and brands the final product.

concepts.name: The St. Gallen Management Model (SGMM)
concepts.simple: A map of everything around a firm: the big world (society, nature, technology, economy), the groups that want something from the firm (customers, investors, staff…), and the firm's own processes.
exam: Slide (SGMM version 5.0): value creation processes (**management processes, business processes, support processes**) operate within a system of **stakeholders** (competitors, investors, suppliers, clients, state, employees, media) exchanging e.g. market share, interests, orders, value, taxes, salary, information, in the environment **society, nature, technology, politics, law**.

Textbook (task perspective, Rüegg-Stürm & Grand 2020): **environmental spheres** (society, nature, technology, economy) → **stakeholders** (actors placing demands on the organization; management must ensure their **cohesion**) → **interaction issues** (resources; norms and values; concerns and interests) → **processes** (business processes = service creation, service innovation, customer processes; management processes = steering; support processes = indirect support, e.g. finance, HR) → **structuring forces** (governance, strategy, structure, culture) → **development modes** (**optimization** of current operations vs. **renewal** challenging the status quo).
concepts.example: A newly developed production technology (technology sphere) forces a firm to change production; job cuts then affect its societal environment.

concepts.name: The economic problem firms solve; division of labour
concepts.simple: People always want more than there is. Firms organise work so that limited resources meet as many needs as possible. Splitting work into small specialised tasks makes everyone much faster.
exam: - Needs and desires **regularly exceed** available resources; **firms coordinate value creation processes** to meet demand with limited resources.

- **Organizational efficiency results from the division of labour and specialization**: Adam Smith, *Wealth of Nations* (**1776**); Ford's **assembly-line production (1913)**; the Formula 1 **pit stop** (highly specialized division of labour).
- Sources of gains: **economies of scale** (advantages of size) and **economies of learning** (advantages of practice).
concepts.example: A pit-stop crew of specialists changes four tyres in seconds; one person doing everything would take minutes.

concepts.name: Taylor and business administration as an empirical science
concepts.simple: Taylor measured how workers did their jobs to find better ways. Today business research looks for patterns in how firms, workers, managers and customers behave.
concepts.exam: Frederick **Taylor**, *The Principles of Scientific Management* (**1911**): the first scientific business studies, focused on **productivity gains**. Business success is driven by **identifiable patterns of human behaviour** (why some firms are more profitable; how employees work together; how managers decide; how consumers respond; how competitors act). → Business administration is an **empirical science** aiming at **generalizable insights**.
concepts.example: Mock exam trap: Smith = 1776 (division of labour); Taylor = 1911 (scientific management); Coase = 1937.

concepts.name: Firm boundaries: why not one giant firm?
concepts.simple: If organising inside a firm is so good, why isn't there one huge company that makes everything? Because organising also has costs.
concepts.exam: The slide lists the largest Swiss companies by market capitalization (Roche ≈ USD 358 bn, Novartis ≈ 292 bn, Nestlé ≈ 257 bn, ABB, UBS…) and asks: **why isn't there a big company that just makes everything?** → firm boundaries depend on the **costs of organizing** vs. the costs of using the market (next concepts).
concepts.example: Even Nestlé buys packaging, trucks and software from other firms.

concepts.name: Costs of organizing: coordination and motivation problems
concepts.simple: When work is split up, someone has to coordinate who does what, and people's own goals may differ from the firm's. A small change in shop sales can turn into huge swings in factory orders: the bullwhip effect.
exam: - **Coordination problem:** who does what, when, and with whom? Division of labour creates coordination needs among specialized units. Example: the **bullwhip effect** (Hau, Padmanabhan, Whang 1997): a supermarket sells 1,000 Coke bottles a week; demand rises 10 % → orders upstream to the bottling plant rise by **more than 10 %** (fluctuations amplify along the supply chain).

- **Motivation problem:** individual and organizational goals are at odds: who bears the burden, who benefits? Reference: **Lazear (2000), *Performance Pay and Productivity*** (mock exam: the Safelite example illustrates a motivation problem addressed by performance pay).
concepts.example: Each stage (shop, wholesaler, bottler) adds a safety margin to its orders, so the 10 % rise grows at every step.

concepts.name: Transaction cost economics (Coase)
concepts.simple: Buying something on the market isn't free: you must search, negotiate, check and fix problems. Coase said firms exist because sometimes doing it yourself is cheaper than all that hassle.
exam: **Neoclassical assumptions:** homogeneous goods; many sellers and buyers without market power; **complete information** about prices, qualities, alternatives; **absence of transaction costs**. In such a world prices coordinate everything, so firms would have no reason to exist.

**Ronald Coase** (father of TCE, Nobel 1991; *The Nature of the Firm*, 1937): **every transaction incurs costs** for **initiation, negotiation, execution, monitoring and adjustment**. Whether a transaction occurs **through the market (externally sourced)** or **within the firm (internally sourced)** depends on **where these transaction costs are lower**.
concepts.example: Mock exam: ‘depreciation’ is NOT a transaction cost type.

concepts.name: Market vs. hierarchy: the make-or-buy decision
concepts.simple: For simple, small things, buying is cheapest. For big, complex, special things, making them yourself becomes cheaper, because contracting on the market gets very messy.
concepts.exam: For every transaction managers decide **make (hierarchy) or buy (market)**: is making relatively more economical than buying? Graph (Coase 1937): x-axis = **scale, scope and complexity of the transaction**, y-axis = transaction costs. **Market (buy)** costs = initiation, negotiation, execution, monitoring, adjustment: **low at first, rising fast** with complexity. **Hierarchy (make)** costs = internal coordination, **inefficiency due to a lack of competitive pressure**, risk taking: **higher at the start but rising more slowly**. Above the intersection, making is cheaper.
concepts.example: Office paper → buy; a component tailored to your secret product → maybe make.

concepts.name: Vertical integration: the Tesla example
concepts.simple: Tesla makes its own batteries and chips instead of just buying them. Taking over earlier steps of your supply chain is called backward integration.
concepts.exam: Tesla builds Gigafactories (e.g. Nevada) and its own chips, although specialized suppliers could do it more cheaply. Musk (2020): Tesla designs and builds much more of the car than other OEMs that use “**catalog engineering**”. Types: **no integration**, **forward integration** (towards customers), **backward integration** (towards suppliers). Gains: **economies of scope** and **economies of learning**. Industry trend: automakers plan to manufacture key components themselves (Reuters 2022).
concepts.example: Tesla producing its own batteries = **backward** vertical integration (mock exam Q12).

concepts.name: Asset specificity, uncertainty, frequency and the hold-up problem
concepts.simple: If you build a machine that only works for one customer, that customer can later squeeze you: “lower your price, or I leave and your machine is worthless.” That's hold-up.
exam: Three drivers of transaction costs and hold-up:
- **Asset specificity:** degree to which investments or services can be used **only for a specific transaction**.
- **Uncertainty:** degree to which future conditions, actions or outcomes cannot be reliably predicted.
- **Frequency:** number of times / regularity with which a transaction is repeated.

**Hold-up problem:** when asset specificity is high, one party may be exposed to the other's **opportunism after an investment has been made**; the other can demand renegotiation because switching would be too costly.

Tesla: battery technology tailored to its vehicles (**asset specificity**); few specialized battery makers (**hold-up risk**); fast-changing technology and demand (**uncertainty**, hard to write complete contracts); huge numbers of cells (**frequency**) → in-house manufacturing reduces transaction costs more than external suppliers can offer.
concepts.example: Mock exam: a mould that can only make one door panel for one car model = high asset specificity.

concepts.name: Game-theoretic model of hold-up (backward induction)
concepts.simple: Think ahead: if the supplier invests, the carmaker will exploit it. Knowing that, the supplier doesn't invest. Both end up worse off than if they could trust each other.
exam: A = supplier with transaction-specific investment; B = automaker. Payoffs (A ; B):
| A's move | B's move | Payoff |
| invest | no exploitation | (10 ; 10) |
| invest | exploitation | (0 ; 20) |
| no investment | – | (5 ; 5) |

**Backward induction:** if A invests, B prefers exploitation (20 > 10) → A would get 0 < 5 → A does not invest. **Subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium: B exploits → A does not invest → (5 ; 5)** ⇒ **underinvestment problem** (both lose compared with (10 ; 10)).
concepts.example: Mock exam: with a contract penalty P on exploitation, B gets 20 − P; B strictly prefers not to exploit when 20 − P < 10, i.e. **P > 10**.

concepts.name: Outlook: Williamson and hybrid governance
concepts.simple: Between ‘buy on the market’ and ‘do it yourself’ there's a middle way: cooperating with partners.
concepts.exam: Is hold-up a compelling reason for a make decision? **Oliver Williamson** (1985, Nobel 2009): transaction costs as a function of **asset specificity**: **market** (cost of contracting) cheapest at low specificity, **hybrid** (cost of cooperation) at medium, **hierarchy** (cost of organizing) at high specificity. → Lecture 2.
concepts.example: A long-term supply alliance is a hybrid between a one-off purchase and a merger.

concepts.name: Punchline
concepts.simple: Firms create value; splitting work makes them productive; but organising costs money, so firms must decide carefully what to do themselves and what to buy.
concepts.exam: (1) **Firms as value creation engines** (productivity). (2) **Division of labour → productivity** (division of labour & specialization). (3) **Make-or-buy decisions** (transaction costs; market vs. hierarchy along scope, scale and complexity). Firms must **weigh the efficiency gains and the transaction costs** from the division of labour.
concepts.example: One-sentence exam answer: firms exist because, for some transactions, coordinating inside the hierarchy is cheaper than using the market (Coase).

connections: **Microeconomics 1.2 ↔ BA 1:** Smith's division of labour and specialization; the **hold-up problem** appears in both (trade dependencies; supplier investments).
**Microeconomics 2.1 ↔ BA 1:** the neoclassical assumptions (homogeneous goods, price takers, complete information) are exactly what TCE relaxes by adding transaction costs.
**Lecture 1 → 2:** Williamson's graph introduces **hybrid governance** (alliances, networks, platforms).
**Asset specificity → Lecture 2:** termination rights and upfront payments as safeguards in alliances.
**SGMM → whole course:** strategy (capture value), innovation (create), marketing (deliver), supply chain (orchestrate).

questions: Define value (benefit minus costs of all production steps) and the value creation process.
Explain why firms exist (Coase) and the make-or-buy logic (market vs. hierarchy graph).
Name the transaction cost types (initiation, negotiation, execution, monitoring, adjustment).
Coordination vs. motivation problems; bullwhip effect (orders rise by more than demand).
Asset specificity, uncertainty, frequency and the hold-up problem; apply to a case (Tesla).
Solve the hold-up game by backward induction; compute the penalty that prevents exploitation.
Author–year pairs: Smith 1776, Taylor 1911, Ford 1913, Coase 1937, Williamson 1985.
traps: In a world matching neoclassical assumptions, firms would have **no reason to exist**.
Hierarchy curve: **starts higher, rises more slowly** than the market curve.
Bullwhip: upstream orders rise by **more** than the change in final demand.
Equilibrium of the hold-up game = **(5 ; 5)**, not (10 ; 10).
mistakes: Confusing economies of scale (size), scope (several products) and learning (experience).
Calling the motivation problem a coordination problem (Lazear/Safelite = motivation).
Forgetting that hold-up arises **after** the specific investment.

memorize: **Value** = customer benefit − costs of all steps required to produce it.
**Value creation process:** resources (labour, capital, knowledge, materials) → transformation → products, services, solutions → perceived value.
**SGMM:** environmental spheres, stakeholders, interaction issues, processes (management, business, support), structuring forces, development modes.
**Division of labour:** Smith 1776; Ford assembly line 1913; Taylor scientific management 1911.
**Costs of organizing:** coordination problem (bullwhip effect) and motivation problem (Lazear 2000).
**Coase (1937):** transaction costs of initiation, negotiation, execution, monitoring, adjustment; make if internal costs are lower.
**Hierarchy costs:** internal coordination, inefficiency from lack of competitive pressure, risk taking.
**Asset specificity / uncertainty / frequency** → transaction costs and hold-up.
**Hold-up:** after a specific investment, the other party can demand renegotiation because switching is too costly.
**Hold-up game:** SPNE = B exploits → A does not invest → (5 ; 5) → underinvestment.

The **Safelite** example is not on the slides (only the Lazear 2000 reference); it appears in your mock exam.

questions.question:
Supplier A decides whether to make a transaction-specific investment. If A invests, automaker B decides whether to exploit A. Payoffs (A ; B): invest & no exploitation (10 ; 10); invest & exploitation (0 ; 20); no investment (5 ; 5).
(a) Solve the game by backward induction and state the subgame-perfect outcome. (b) Explain why this is called an underinvestment problem. (c) A contract specifies a penalty P that B pays to A if B exploits (B gets 20 − P, A gets 0 + P). From which P on does B not exploit, and what does A then do?
questions.model: (a) Last stage: if A invested, B compares 20 (exploit) with 10 (no exploitation) → B exploits. First stage: A anticipates this and compares 0 (invest, exploited) with 5 (no investment) → A does not invest. SPNE: B would exploit; A does not invest → (5 ; 5). (b) Both would be better off with investment and no exploitation (10 ; 10 > 5 ; 5), but the hold-up threat makes A refrain from the value-creating specific investment → underinvestment. (c) B does not exploit if 20 − P < 10 ⇔ P > 10 (at P = 10 B is indifferent). Then A, anticipating no exploitation, gets 10 > 5 by investing → A invests; outcome (10 ; 10).

keyPoints.text: (a) B's choice at the last stage: exploit (20 > 10)
(b) Pareto-better (10 ; 10) not reached because of hold-up → underinvestment

questions.question: Using transaction cost economics, explain why Tesla produces its own batteries although specialized suppliers could produce them more cheaply. Refer to all three transaction characteristics.
questions.model: TCE: a transaction is carried out where transaction costs are lower (market vs. hierarchy). Asset specificity: Tesla's battery technology is closely tailored to its vehicles and energy concept → high specificity → hold-up risk with few specialized battery makers (high dependence, renegotiation risk). Uncertainty: rapidly evolving technology and demand make comprehensive contracts hard to draft → high contracting costs. Frequency: Tesla needs a very large number of cells → recurring coordination costs with external suppliers. Together, vertical (backward) integration reduces transaction costs more than the production-cost advantage of external suppliers.
